findings.title: Overview of rural and small towns water services in Northern Region
findings.summary: The 2014 service monitoring round assessed rural and small towns water services in Northern Region of Ghana.

findings.title: Aquifer storage and recharge suitability in northern Ghana
findings.summary: Most of the study area has static water levels from 10 to 70 m, suitable for aquifer storage and recharge techniques.

findings.title: Flood impacts on water quality in Tamale
findings.summary: Floods deteriorate water quality of unprotected sources in Tamale, increasing faecal contamination risks.

findings.title: Tamale-Damongo Water Supply Project financing and progress
findings.summary: Ghana Water Limited is advancing the €312 million Tamale-Damongo Water Supply Project with EU and other partners' funding.

findings.title: Access to improved drinking-water in Ghana
findings.summary: Urban population access to improved drinking water increased from 73% in 2016 to 83% in 2018 in Ghana.

findings.title: Basement aquifers characteristics in Ghana
findings.summary: Basement aquifers have transmissivity between 0.2 and 119 m²/day and borehole depths from 40 to 200 m.

findings.title: Flood hazards in Northern Ghana including Tamale
findings.summary: Northern Region is among the most flood-prone areas in Ghana, with floods causing significant national impacts.

findings.title: Tamale water system project plans
findings.summary: Plans include building a pumping station at Yapei to produce about 30 million gallons of water for Tamale Metropolis.

findings.title: Water service level standards in Ghana
findings.summary: Water service standards include a maximum distance of 500 metres to the farthest household for rural water schemes.

findings.title: Groundwater aquifers in northern Ghana
findings.summary: Aquifers in northern Ghana are semi-confined with depths ranging from 10 to 60 m, recharged mainly by precipitation.

findings.title: Local climate change impacts in Tamale
findings.summary: Tamale residents report floods (48%), increasing temperatures (15%), and erratic rainfall (13.8%) as climate change impacts.

findings.title: Government plans for Tamale water project construction
findings.summary: Government budgeted for a pumping station on the White Volta at Yapei to supply additional water to Tamale.

findings.title: Household water sources and storage in Northern Ghana
findings.summary: Over half the population depend on surface water sources often contaminated with faecal matter in Northern Ghana.

findings.title: Groundwater availability for irrigation in northeast Ghana
findings.summary: Groundwater levels are usually shallow, making it relatively easy to abstract water by hand digging shallow wells.

findings.title: Research on local adaptation to climate change in Tamale
findings.summary: Studies document grassroots coping strategies for climate change impacts in Tamale, Northern Ghana.

findings.title: Government to locally fund Tamale water project after funding delay
findings.summary: Government will mobilize local funds to execute the Tamale water supply project after €277 million facility delay.

Households: 161,115 mapped buildings (every building OpenStreetMap has in the analysis area) grouped into 53,829 clusters of 50 m, at 3.6 people per building (census household size, one household per building) and 20 L per person per day.

Today: each cluster walks to the nearest of 4 water points people can use (3 surveyed working in WPdx+, the rest wells, boreholes, springs and taps mapped in OpenStreetMap) along streets and footpaths at 3.49 km/h. Clusters with none within reach are assumed to spend 60 minutes per round trip at an unmapped source. 377 surveyed points reported broken are the rehabilitation targets.

New taps are sited one at a time where they save the most walking for people not yet served, 250 people each (Sphere Handbook 2018, Water supply standard 2.1); queues follow from a 7.5 L/min tap. Pipes follow the streets from the tank.
A cluster uses a new tap only when its round trip, queue included, beats today's. Queues at existing points are not modelled because their real capacity is unmapped.

Futures: 24 seeded ten-year runs per stress-tested project. Existing points are out of service 16% of the time, the new system 10%; repairs take 3-9 weeks; households grow 2.8% a year; rainfall varies up to 20% a year and rainwater storage is simulated week by week.

A future holds when people served over ten years average at least 80% of the design figure. The recommendation is the lowest whole-life cost per person served among projects that hold in at least 70% of futures.
Whole-life cost is capital plus 10 years of operation and maintenance, including trucked water and filter consumables where they apply (demo planning assumption planning figures).
Maintenance matters: with professional maintenance this project holds in 22 of 24 futures; community-managed, with repairs taking 14-42 weeks, it would hold in 3.

Existing points are out of service 16% of the time (Schultes et al. (2022), Longitudinal borehole functionality in 15 rural Ghanaian towns, BMC Research Notes ("BH functionality rates ranged between 81 and 87%")) and take 3-9 weeks to repair (central: Oxford REACH Kitui maintenance policy brief (handpumps 43 days without professional maintenance); low: FundiFix baseline ("over 30 days"); high: Stanford/Whave Uganda ("can exceed 150 days")).

The new system breaks down as often as community-managed schemes of its type (motorised: every 293 days; handpump: every 129 days), but with professional maintenance it is back within the week (FundiFix, Kenya (98% of repairs within three days); Whave, Uganda (repair by end of next day); REACH ("less than two days")).
Households grow 2.8% a year (World Bank World Development Indicators (2025)).
requiredValidation: Hydrogeological review and ground geophysical survey (resistivity or TEM) at the shortlisted point before any commitment.
Exploratory drilling with lithological logging and step-drawdown plus constant-rate pumping tests to establish sustainable yield.
Water-quality testing against national and WHO standards, including bacteriological, fluoride, arsenic, nitrate and salinity.
Land ownership confirmation and legal right of access or easement for the site and the pipeline corridor.
Community consultation on siting, tariff, and the operation and maintenance model, including who holds the spares.
Seasonal access verification — confirm the approach is passable for rigs and delivery vehicles in the wet season.
Environmental and social review, including abstraction licensing and downstream or aquifer impact.
Final engineering design, bill of quantities and competitive tender.

projects.label: Rehabilitation of the existing borehole
projects.anchor: Restores a broken borehole (Hand Pump - India Mark, reported broken 2014)

assumptions: Households: 161,115 mapped buildings (every building OpenStreetMap has in the analysis area) grouped into 53,829 clusters of 50 m, at 3.6 people per building (census household size, one household per building) and 20 L per person per day.

Today: each cluster walks to the nearest of 4 water points people can use (3 surveyed working in WPdx+, the rest wells, boreholes, springs and taps mapped in OpenStreetMap) along streets and footpaths at 3.49 km/h. Clusters with none within reach are assumed to spend 60 minutes per round trip at an unmapped source. 377 surveyed points reported broken are the rehabilitation targets.

New taps are sited one at a time where they save the most walking for people not yet served, 250 people each (Sphere Handbook 2018, Water supply standard 2.1); queues follow from a 7.5 L/min tap. Pipes follow the streets from the tank.
A cluster uses a new tap only when its round trip, queue included, beats today's. Queues at existing points are not modelled because their real capacity is unmapped.

Futures: 24 seeded ten-year runs per stress-tested project. Existing points are out of service 16% of the time, the new system 10%; repairs take 3-9 weeks; households grow 2.8% a year; rainfall varies up to 20% a year and rainwater storage is simulated week by week.

A future holds when people served over ten years average at least 80% of the design figure. The recommendation is the lowest whole-life cost per person served among projects that hold in at least 70% of futures.
Whole-life cost is capital plus 10 years of operation and maintenance, including trucked water and filter consumables where they apply (demo planning assumption planning figures).
Maintenance matters: with professional maintenance this project holds in 22 of 24 futures; community-managed, with repairs taking 14-42 weeks, it would hold in 3.

Existing points are out of service 16% of the time (Schultes et al. (2022), Longitudinal borehole functionality in 15 rural Ghanaian towns, BMC Research Notes ("BH functionality rates ranged between 81 and 87%")) and take 3-9 weeks to repair (central: Oxford REACH Kitui maintenance policy brief (handpumps 43 days without professional maintenance); low: FundiFix baseline ("over 30 days"); high: Stanford/Whave Uganda ("can exceed 150 days")).

The new system breaks down as often as community-managed schemes of its type (motorised: every 293 days; handpump: every 129 days), but with professional maintenance it is back within the week (FundiFix, Kenya (98% of repairs within three days); Whave, Uganda (repair by end of next day); REACH ("less than two days")).
Households grow 2.8% a year (World Bank World Development Indicators (2025)).

narrative: 275 of 320 sites near Tamale passed all hard constraints; the recommended site scores 60% (161 m from a road, 7 buildings within 400 m). A solar-powered borehole with storage and tap stands at $24,000–$56,000 would serve 4,192–6,652 people. Pre-feasibility only — field validation required.
